https://www.dw.com/en/hurricane-isaias-m.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O5sS Isaias brings the risk of flooding to low-lying areas of Florida's Gulf coast Image: Chris Urso/REUTERS Advertisement Hurricane Isaias has made landfall as a Category 2 storm near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Friday evening. Destin is in the panhandle region of northern Florida. What do we know about Hurricane Isaias? The NHC warned of "life-threatening storm surge impacting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland." The weather system is also bringing extreme winds, with a tornado watch issued for parts of Florida and southern Georgia. Isaias is packing sustained winds of up to 105 miles per hour Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP After the storm made landfall, the Florida Division of Emergency Management said the tornado watch for parts of North Florida has been extended until at least 6 a.m. local time Saturday (10 a.m. UTC). The NHC said the hurricane has maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (165 kilometers per hour). The storm is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season and was originally a strong Category 3 storm before making landfall. It is expected to weaken as it passes over land. The storm has downed trees in Pensacola in the Florida panhandle Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP Evacuations took place in coastal communities as the hurricane approached. Florida, Georgia and Alabama have all declared a State of Emergency due to the extreme weather system. US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said "emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to #Isaias." Florida Governor DeSantis urges residents to 'buckle down' In a press conference, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis urged residents to "buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads." Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned those "thinking about using this storm's power outages and evacuations to break in, loot, or steal: don't even try it." "During an emergency, these crimes become first-degree felonies, punishable by up to 30 years in prison," Uthmeier said. People boarded up businesses ahead of the storm's landfall Image: Marco Bello/REUTERS According to power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, roughly 480,000 customers altogether were without electricity as of Friday evening in Florida, Georgia and Alabama. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said Uber, Comcast and Home Depot have offered to help Alabamians during the storm. Uber, for example, is offering free round-trip rides to state-approved evacuation shelters in Mobile and Baldwin counties.
